title: Why Does the WRONG Finger Move? 🤞
description:
Cross your wrists, clasp your fingers and roll your hands in. Now wiggle the finger you're looking at. Wrong one, right? Very often the finger that moves is its twin: the same finger on your OTHER hand. Your brain picks a hand by which side it sees it on, and crossing your wrists swapped the sides. But if someone TOUCHES the finger instead of pointing at it, you almost never miss.

Did the right finger move?

The science: this is the hand-reversal illusion, already called the "Japanese illusion" in papers from 1929 and 1935. With the hands cross-folded, people asked to lift a finger someone points at often lift the matching finger of the other hand; when the finger is touched instead, mistakes almost never happen (Van Riper, American Journal of Psychology, 1935, as reported and replicated by Hong, Xu, Kang and Tong, Frontiers in Integrative Neuroscience, 2012; BrainFacts.org / Society for Neuroscience, 2021). The usual explanation is a clash between what your eyes see and where your body feels your hands; Hong and colleagues found the twisted hands stay slower even with the eyes closed, so the swapped posture itself plays a part too. The coloured hands and the 'call' up the arm are pictures of the idea, not real parts of your body.
